claim: The vertebrate eye primordium consists of a pseudostratified neuroepithelium called the optic vesicle (OV).
source: The vertebrate eye primordium consists of a pseudostratified neuroepithelium, the optic vesicle (OV), in which cells acquire neural retina or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) fates.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational description of the eye primordium structure.

claim: In the optic vesicle, cells acquire neural retina or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) fates.
source: The vertebrate eye primordium consists of a pseudostratified neuroepithelium, the optic vesicle (OV), in which cells acquire neural retina or retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) fates.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract describing cell fate specification in the OV.

claim: As neural retina and RPE fates arise, the optic vesicle assumes a cup shape.
source: As these fates arise, the OV assumes a cup shape, influenced by mechanical forces generated within the neural retina.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract describing the morphological transformation of the OV.

claim: The cup shape of the optic vesicle is influenced by mechanical forces generated within the neural retina.
source: As these fates arise, the OV assumes a cup shape, influenced by mechanical forces generated within the neural retina.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract as a known mechanism of OV morphogenesis.

claim: The Tg(E1-bhlhe40:GFP) zebrafish line was generated to track RPE morphogenesis.
source: We generated a zebrafish Tg(E1-bhlhe40:GFP) line to track RPE morphogenesis and interrogate its participation in OV folding.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a key methodological contribution of the study.

claim: In zebrafish, RPE cells stretch and flatten in virtual absence of proliferation during optic cup formation.
source: We show that, in virtual absence of proliferation, RPE cells stretch and flatten, thereby matching the retinal curvature and promoting OV folding.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: RPE cell stretching and flattening matches the retinal curvature.
source: We show that, in virtual absence of proliferation, RPE cells stretch and flatten, thereby matching the retinal curvature and promoting OV folding.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: RPE cell stretching and flattening promotes optic vesicle folding.
source: We show that, in virtual absence of proliferation, RPE cells stretch and flatten, thereby matching the retinal curvature and promoting OV folding.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by experimental manipulations.

claim: Localized interference with the RPE cytoskeleton disrupts tissue stretching.
source: Localized interference with the RPE cytoskeleton disrupts tissue stretching and OV folding.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as an experimental finding.

claim: Localized interference with the RPE cytoskeleton disrupts optic vesicle folding.
source: Localized interference with the RPE cytoskeleton disrupts tissue stretching and OV folding.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as an experimental finding.

claim: Extreme RPE flattening and accelerated differentiation are efficient solutions adopted by fast-developing species to enable timely optic cup formation.
source: Thus, extreme RPE flattening and accelerated differentiation are efficient solutions adopted by fast-developing species to enable timely optic cup formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the comparative analysis across species.

claim: In amniotes, proliferation drives RPE expansion with a much-reduced need of cell flattening.
source: This mechanism differs in amniotes, in which proliferation drives RPE expansion with a much-reduced need of cell flattening.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a comparative finding between zebrafish and amniotes.

claim: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is composed of a monolayer of pigment-enriched epithelial cells abutting the neural retina.
source: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is an essential component of the vertebrate eye, composed of a monolayer of pigment-enriched epithelial cells abutting the neural retina (NR) with a primary role in photoreception (Letelier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the description.

claim: The RPE has a primary role in photoreception.
source: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is an essential component of the vertebrate eye, composed of a monolayer of pigment-enriched epithelial cells abutting the neural retina (NR) with a primary role in photoreception (Letelier et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Letelier et al., 2017.

claim: RPE cells have a neural origin.
source: Despite the acquisition of specialized epithelial properties, RPE cells have a neural origin and share progenitors with the NR.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: RPE cells share progenitors with the neural retina.
source: Despite the acquisition of specialized epithelial properties, RPE cells have a neural origin and share progenitors with the NR.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: In amniotes, the optic vesicles appear as balloon-like structures positioned at the sides of the anterior neural tube.
source: In amniotes, the OVs appear as balloon-like structures positioned at the sides of the anterior neural tube (Moreno-Marmol et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Moreno-Marmol et al., 2018.

claim: In zebrafish, optic vesicles are flat and form two bi-layered structures with the outer and inner layers distally connected by a rim or hinge.
source: In zebrafish instead, these primordia are flat and form two bi-layered structures with the outer and inner layers distally connected by a rim or hinge (Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Li et al., 2000.

claim: Under the influence of inductive signals, the two layers of the optic vesicle activate different genetic programs that specify cells as neural retina or RPE.
source: Under the influence of inductive signals (Gallardo and Bovolenta, 2018; Cardozo et al., 2020), the two layers activate different genetic programs that specify the cells of the inner layer and ventral outer layer as NR and those of the dorsal outer layer as RPE (Beccari et al., 2013; Buono and Martinez-Morales, 2020; Buono et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Whilst specification occurs, the optic vesicle bends assuming a cup-like shape.
source: Whilst this specification occurs, the OV bends assuming a cup-like shape (Martinez-Morales et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Martinez-Morales et al., 2017.

claim: The ojoplano medaka fish mutant affects a transmembrane protein localized at the basal end feet of neural retina cells.
source: The discovery of the ojoplano medaka fish mutant – affecting a transmembrane protein localized at the basal end feet of NR cells (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009) – in which the OV remains unfolded, was instrumental to propose that basal constriction of NR progenitors is at the basis of OV bending (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Martinez-Morales et al., 2009.

claim: In the ojoplano medaka fish mutant, the optic vesicle remains unfolded.
source: The discovery of the ojoplano medaka fish mutant – affecting a transmembrane protein localized at the basal end feet of NR cells (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009) – in which the OV remains unfolded, was instrumental to propose that basal constriction of NR progenitors is at the basis of OV bending (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Martinez-Morales et al., 2009.

claim: Basal constriction of neural retina progenitors is at the basis of optic vesicle bending.
source: The discovery of the ojoplano medaka fish mutant – affecting a transmembrane protein localized at the basal end feet of NR cells (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009) – in which the OV remains unfolded, was instrumental to propose that basal constriction of NR progenitors is at the basis of OV bending (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Martinez-Morales et al., 2009.

claim: Basal constriction is mediated by the redistribution of the actomyosin cytoskeleton.
source: This basal constriction is mediated by the redistribution of the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Nicolas-Perez et al., 2016; Bryan et al., 2016), which also enables the apical relaxation of retinal cells (Sidhaye and Norden, 2017), enhanced by focal adhesions of the apical surface with the extracellular matrix molecules (ECM) such as laminin (Bryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the mechanism.

claim: Actomyosin cytoskeleton redistribution enables the apical relaxation of retinal cells.
source: This basal constriction is mediated by the redistribution of the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Nicolas-Perez et al., 2016; Bryan et al., 2016), which also enables the apical relaxation of retinal cells (Sidhaye and Norden, 2017), enhanced by focal adhesions of the apical surface with the extracellular matrix molecules (ECM) such as laminin (Bryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Sidhaye and Norden, 2017.

claim: Apical relaxation is enhanced by focal adhesions of the apical surface with extracellular matrix molecules such as laminin.
source: This basal constriction is mediated by the redistribution of the actomyosin cytoskeleton (Martinez-Morales et al., 2009; Nicolas-Perez et al., 2016; Bryan et al., 2016), which also enables the apical relaxation of retinal cells (Sidhaye and Norden, 2017), enhanced by focal adhesions of the apical surface with the extracellular matrix molecules (ECM) such as laminin (Bryan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Bryan et al., 2016.

claim: The acquisition of apical convexity and basal concavity in the neural retina epithelium are accepted drivers of the biomechanical forces that induce optic vesicle folding.
source: Nevertheless and independently of their relative contribution, the acquisition of apical convexity and basal concavity in the NR epithelium are accepted drivers of the biomechanical forces that induce OV folding (Okuda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Okuda et al., 2018.

claim: In zebrafish, optic vesicle folding is reinforced by rim involution or epithelial flow.
source: In zebrafish, this mechanism is reinforced by rim involution or epithelial flow, a process whereby progenitors at the hinge emit dynamic lamellipodia at the basal side and actively translocate from the ventral outer layer of the OV into the inner/retinal layer (Li et al., 2000; Sidhaye and Norden, 2017; Zheng et al., 2000; Heermann et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the mechanism.

claim: During rim involution, progenitors at the hinge emit dynamic lamellipodia at the basal side and actively translocate from the ventral outer layer into the inner/retinal layer.
source: In zebrafish, this mechanism is reinforced by rim involution or epithelial flow, a process whereby progenitors at the hinge emit dynamic lamellipodia at the basal side and actively translocate from the ventral outer layer of the OV into the inner/retinal layer (Li et al., 2000; Sidhaye and Norden, 2017; Zheng et al., 2000; Heermann et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2012; Picker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations describing the process.

claim: Periocular neural crest cells facilitate rim involution, in part by the deposition of the extracellular matrix.
source: Periocular neural crest cells appear to facilitate this flow, in part by the deposition of the ECM (Bryan et al., 2020) to which the lamellipodia attach (Sidhaye and Norden, 2017; Heermann et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Bryan et al., 2020 and others.

claim: Rim involution results in an unbalanced cell number between the two layers, which should favour neural retina bending.
source: The result of this flow is an unbalanced cell number between the two layers, which should favour NR bending (Sidhaye and Norden, 2017; Heermann et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the inference.

claim: As the optic vesicle folds, the pseudostratified neuroepithelial cells of the dorsal outer layer progressively align their nuclei becoming a cuboidal monolayer in amniote species.
source: Indeed as the OV folds, the pseudostratified neuroepithelial cells of the OV dorsal outer layer progressively align their nuclei becoming a cuboidal monolayer in amniotes species (Moreno-Marmol et al., 2018; Martinez-Morales et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Moreno-Marmol et al., 2018 and Martinez-Morales et al., 2004.

claim: In zebrafish, cuboidal RPE cells further differentiate to a flat/squamous epithelium.
source: In zebrafish, cuboidal cells further differentiate to a flat/squamous epithelium (Zheng et al., 2000; Kwan et al., 2012) that spreads to cover the whole apical surface of the NR (Zheng et al., 2000; Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Zheng et al., 2000 and Kwan et al., 2012.

claim: In mice, failure of RPE specification enables RPE progenitors to acquire a neural retina fate.
source: In mice, failure of RPE specification, as observed after genetic inactivation of key specifier genes (i.e. Otx1/Otx2, Mitf, Yap/Taz), enables RPE progenitors to acquire an NR fate (Martinez-Morales et al., 2001; Bharti et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2001, Bharti et al., 2006, and Kim et al., 2016.

claim: Optic cups with failed RPE specification present evident folding defects.
source: The resulting optic cups (OCs) present evident folding defects (Martinez-Morales et al., 2001), raising the possibility that specific RPE features are needed for OC formation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Martinez-Morales et al., 2001.

claim: A differential stiffness of the RPE vs. the neural retina layer has been proposed to drive the self-organization of mammalian organoids into an optic cup.
source: In line with this idea, a differential stiffness of the RPE vs. the NR layer has been proposed to drive the self-organization of mammalian organoids into an OC (Eiraku et al., 2011; Okuda et al., 2018; Nakano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Eiraku et al., 2011, Okuda et al., 2018, and Nakano et al., 2012.

claim: Generation of proper RPE cell numbers seems a requirement for correct optic cup folding in mice.
source: Furthermore, generation of proper RPE cell numbers seems a requirement for correct OC folding in mice (Carpenter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Carpenter et al., 2015.

claim: The E40 (bhlhe40) gene encodes a basic helix-loop-helix family member that is a light and hypoxia-induced transcription factor.
source: The E40 (bhlhe40) gene, a basic helix-loop-helix family member, encodes a light and hypoxia-induced transcription factor (also known as Dec1, Stra13, Sharp2, or Bhlhb2) involved in cell proliferation and differentiation as well as in the control of circadian rhythms (Yamada and Miyamoto, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Yamada and Miyamoto, 2005.

claim: In neurulating zebrafish embryos, bhlhe40 expression is limited to cells of the prospective RPE.
source: In neurulating zebrafish embryos, its expression is limited to cells of the prospective RPE (Figure 1A; Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017; Yao et al., 2006), representing a potentially suitable tissue marker.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017 and Yao et al., 2006, and supported by Figure 1A.

claim: The E1 enhancer drove specific and restricted GFP reporter expression into the prospective RPE.
source: Only the E1 enhancer drove specific and restricted GFP reporter expression into the prospective RPE.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the generation of the transgenic line.

claim: The Tg(E1-bhlhe40:GFP) transgenic line faithfully recapitulated the bhlhe40 mRNA expression profile.
source: Time-lapse studies of the Tg(E1-bhlhe40:GFP) progeny confirmed that the transgenic line faithfully recapitulated the bhlhe40 mRNA expression profile detected with ISH (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparison of Figure 1A and 1C.

claim: GFP reporter expression appeared in a discrete group of neuroepithelial cells in the dorso-medial region of the optic vesicle at 16-17 hpf.
source: GFP reporter expression appeared in a discrete group of neuroepithelial cells in the dorso-medial region of the OV (16–17 hpf) and expanded both posteriorly and ventrally (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 1 and Figure 1—video 2), so that, by 24 hpf, GFP-positive cells appeared to wrap around the entire inner NR layer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1C and videos.

claim: By 24 hpf, GFP-positive cells appeared to wrap around the entire inner neural retina layer.
source: GFP reporter expression appeared in a discrete group of neuroepithelial cells in the dorso-medial region of the OV (16–17 hpf) and expanded both posteriorly and ventrally (Figure 1C; Figure 1—video 1 and Figure 1—video 2), so that, by 24 hpf, GFP-positive cells appeared to wrap around the entire inner NR layer.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1C and videos.

claim: The overall RPE surface underwent an approximately twofold expansion between 17 and 22 hpf.
source: In parallel, the overall RPE surface underwent an approximately twofold expansion between 17 and 22 hpf (from approximately 1.1–2.2 × 103 μm2; Figure 3C; Figure 1—video 1 and Figure 1—video 2), reflecting the large increase in the apical area observed in each individual cell at later stages (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3C and videos.

claim: Between stages 17 and 21 hpf, the overall thickness of the RPE tissue underwent, on average, a flattening of more than threefold.
source: The combined quantification of the different segments (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showed that, between stages 17 and 21 hpf, the overall thickness of the RPE tissue underwent, on average, a flattening of more than threefold (from a mean of about 24–8 µm; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: The RPE volume only slightly changed between 17 and 20 hpf with a slope increase of 0.47 × 103 μm3/h.
source: In line with the idea that cell flattening is per se sufficient to account for whole tissue enlargement, the RPE volume only slightly changed between 17 and 20 hpf with a slope increase of 0.47 × 103 μm3/h (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: At 30 hpf, RPE cells presented a polygonal, frequently hexagonal, morphology.
source: At 30 hpf, RPE cells presented a polygonal, frequently hexagonal, morphology (Figure 2D and D'), with an apical surface area that, on average, became about eightfold larger than that observed in progenitor (PN) cells (Figure 2F; RPE‾a: 354.8 ± 100.3 μm2 vs. PN‾a: 43.7 ± 7.8 μm2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2D and D'.

claim: At 30 hpf, the apical surface area of RPE cells became about eightfold larger than that observed in progenitor cells.
source: At 30 hpf, RPE cells presented a polygonal, frequently hexagonal, morphology (Figure 2D and D'), with an apical surface area that, on average, became about eightfold larger than that observed in progenitor (PN) cells (Figure 2F; RPE‾a: 354.8 ± 100.3 μm2 vs. PN‾a: 43.7 ± 7.8 μm2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2F.

claim: The abutting apical surface of neural retina cells slightly shrank as compared to that of progenitor cells.
source: In contrast, the abutting apical surface of NR cells slightly shrank as compared to that of PN cells (Figure 2E, E' and F; NR‾a: 22.5 ± 2.9 μm2 vs. PN‾a: 43.7 ± 7.8 μm2) while maintaining a constant apico-basal length.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2E, E' and F.

claim: Photoactivation of azidoblebbistatin in the prospective RPE cells reproduced the phenotype observed upon whole embryo bathing in blebbistatin, in which RPE cells acquired a cuboidal morphology.
source: Notably, Ableb photoactivation in the prospective RPE cells reproduced, although slightly less efficiently (n = 30/44 embryos), the phenotype observed upon whole embryo bathing in blebbistatin, in which RPE cells acquired a cuboidal morphology (Figure 4C, D, G, G').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4.

claim: Failure of cell flattening in the irradiated region of the RPE was consistently associated with a significant reduction of optic vesicle folding.
source: Failure of cell flattening in the irradiated region of the RPE was consistently associated with a significant reduction of OV folding (Figure 4E–G), as assessed by measuring the invagination angle (Sidhaye and Norden, 2017), which was normalized to that of control embryos (Figure 4L; Mann-Whitney U test: z = −2.704, p < 0.01, mean rank for control 21.60 vs. Ableb-treated 33.33).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: Photoactivation of azidoblebbistatin in the prospective neural retina basal region resulted in an elongated neural retina and a significantly impaired optic vesicle folding.
source: Photoactivation of Ableb in similar areas of the prospective NR basal region resulted in an elongated NR and a significantly impaired OV folding (Figure 4J), as determined by the invagination angles normalized to those of control OV (Figure 4N; Mann-Whitney U test: z = −3.035, p < 0.01, mean rank control 10.29 vs. Ableb 20.06).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: Disruption of neural retina morphogenesis had no consequences on RPE development: cells underwent normal flattening with apico-basal lengths comparable to those of controls.
source: Notably, disruption of NR morphogenesis had no consequences on RPE development in all the analysed embryos (n = 16/22): cells underwent normal flattening with apico-basal lengths comparable to those of controls (Figure 4H'–J' and M; Mann-Whitney U test: z = 0.582, p > 0.05, mean rank control 14.50 vs. Ableb 16.38).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4 with statistical analysis.

claim: RPE flattening is not secondary to neural retina folding but rather a tissue autonomous event.
source: These data strongly support that RPE flattening is not secondary to NR folding but rather a tissue autonomous event.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the azidoblebbistatin experiments.

claim: Optic vesicle folding requires forces independently generated in both the neural retina and RPE.
source: They also indicate that OV folding requires forces independently generated in both the NR and RPE.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the experimental manipulations.

claim: In neuroepithelial RPE progenitors, microtubules grew in the apico-basal direction, whereas growth turned to the medio-lateral plane as the RPE cells became squamous.
source: In neuroepithelial RPE progenitors, microtubules grew in the apico-basal direction, whereas growth turned to the medio-lateral plane, as the RPE cells became squamous (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: In the presence of nocodazole, RPE cells retained a columnar-like morphology.
source: The eye of DMSO-treated embryos developed normally (Figure 5B and E), whereas in the presence of nocodazole RPE cells retained a columnar-like morphology with a stronger phenotype in embryos exposed to the drug at an earlier stage (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Nocodazole treatment did not prevent the activation of the GFP reporter expression.
source: Nocodazole treatment did not prevent the activation of the GFP reporter expression (Figure 5C) or the acquisition/distribution of expected specification (otx1 and mitf) and apico-basal polarity (zo-1 and laminin) markers (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: RPE cells expressing STMN1 retained a cuboidal-like shape with an abnormally increased apico-basal axis as compared to GFP-positive cells in control UAS:GFP-injected embryos.
source: RPE cells expressing STMN1 – and notably also those nearby – retained a cuboidal-like shape with an abnormally increased apico-basal axis as compared to GFP-positive cells in control UAS:GFP-injected embryos.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the STMN1 overexpression experiments.

claim: The data derived from the manipulation of the actomyosin and microtubule cytoskeleton suggest that the RPE actively participates in optic vesicle folding by undergoing a tissue autonomous stretching driven by cell cytoskeletal rearrangements.
source: All in all, the data derived from the manipulation of the actomyosin and microtubule cytoskeleton suggest that the RPE actively participates in OV folding by undergoing a tissue autonomous stretching driven by cell cytoskeletal rearrangements.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the cytoskeletal manipulation experiments.

claim: Zebrafish RPE cells barely proliferate during optic vesicle folding.
source: Our finding that the zebrafish RPE largely grows through autonomous cell flattening agrees with the observation that zebrafish RPE cells barely proliferate during OV folding (Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017.

claim: Pharmacological treatment of embryos to block cell division during optic vesicle folding has little or no consequences on RPE expansion.
source: Furthermore, pharmacological treatment of embryos to block cell division during OV folding has little or no consequences on RPE expansion (Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017.

claim: In mouse embryos, RPE proliferation seems a requirement for optic vesicle folding.
source: These observations however differ from reports in mouse embryos, in which RPE proliferation seems a requirement for OV folding (Carpenter et al., 2015) and suggest the existence of species-specific modes of early RPE growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Carpenter et al., 2015.

claim: At 17 hpf, BrdU-positive cells accounted for 49% of the total RPE cells.
source: At the earlier stage (17 hpf), BrdU-positive cells were scattered across the RPE with no easily identifiable geometry and accounted for 49% of the total RPE cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing BrdU incorporation experiments.

claim: The fraction of BrdU-positive RPE cells dropped to about 20% at 19 hpf.
source: This fraction dropped to about 20% at 19 hpf, when cells are flat, and then to 12% at 48 hpf (Figure 6B) when the epithelium is maturing.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 6B.

claim: There is a clear correlation between proliferation rate and developmental stage in zebrafish RPE.
source: Statistical analysis showed significant differences between 17 and 20 hpf (Mann-Whitney U test: z = −2.619, p < 0.01, mean rank for 17 hpf is 8 and for 19 hpf is 3) and a clear correlation between proliferation rate and developmental stage (Kruskal-Wallis test: χ2(df = 7, n = 40) = 32,023; p < 0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical analysis.

claim: Acquisition of RPE identity, cell shape changes, and optic vesicle folding are associated with a progressive reduction of cell proliferation in the optic vesicle outer layer.
source: Thus, acquisition of RPE identity, cell shape changes, and OV folding are associated with a progressive reduction of cell proliferation in the OV outer layer.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the proliferation analysis.

claim: Medaka fish develop slower than zebrafish embryos, so that their optic vesicles take about 8 hr more to reach a fully developed optic cup (26 vs. 18 hr).
source: Notably, medaka fish develop slower than zebrafish embryos, so that, from first appearance, their OVs take about 8 hr more to reach a fully developed OC (26 vs. 18 hr) (Furutani-Seiki and Wittbrodt, 2004), a time compatible with an additional round of cell division.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Furutani-Seiki and Wittbrodt, 2004.

claim: In medaka, about 70% of the cells in the optic vesicle outer layer were actively cycling at st18 to 22-23, and this proportion dropped to about 48% at optic cup stage.
source: Consistent with this idea, BrdU incorporation in st18 to 22–23 medaka embryos showed that about 70% of the cells in the OV outer layer were actively cycling and this proportion dropped to about 48% at OC stage (Figure 7A and E) with a slightly less evident decrease of the average apico-basal axis (st18: 21.3 µm vs. st23 3.5 µm; Figure 7A) as compared to the changes observed in zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7A and E.

claim: In chick and mouse embryos, a similar and almost constant proportion of RPE progenitors incorporated BrdU during optic vesicle to optic cup conversion.
source: An equivalent analysis in chick and mouse embryos showed similar results. In these species OV conversion into an OC takes about 27 and 48 hr, respectively. During this period a similar and almost constant proportion of RPE progenitors incorporated BrdU (Figure 7B, C and E), including when cells acquired the expression of the RPE differentiation marker Otx2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7B, C and E.

claim: In chick, RPE cells only roughly halved their apico-basal axis during optic vesicle to optic cup conversion (HH12: 30.1 µm vs. HH18: 15.8 µm).
source: Furthermore, RPE cells only roughly halved their apico-basal axis (chick: HH12: 30.1 µm vs. HH18: 15.8 µm; mouse: E9.5: 23.7 µm vs. E11.5 13 µm Figure 7B and C), suggesting that in slower developing species, proliferation but not stretching accounts for RPE surface increase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7B and C.

claim: In mouse, RPE cells only roughly halved their apico-basal axis during optic vesicle to optic cup conversion (E9.5: 23.7 µm vs. E11.5 13 µm).
source: Furthermore, RPE cells only roughly halved their apico-basal axis (chick: HH12: 30.1 µm vs. HH18: 15.8 µm; mouse: E9.5: 23.7 µm vs. E11.5 13 µm Figure 7B and C), suggesting that in slower developing species, proliferation but not stretching accounts for RPE surface increase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7B and C.

claim: The human eye primordium is first visible at about 4-5 weeks of gestation corresponding to Carnegie stage (CS)13.
source: The human eye primordium is first visible at about 4–5 weeks of gestation corresponding to Carnegie stage (CS)13 (O'Rahilly, 1983).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to O'Rahilly, 1983.

claim: A fully formed human optic cup is reached roughly 10 days after CS13, at CS16.
source: A fully formed OC is reached only roughly 10 days after, at CS16 (O'Rahilly, 1983).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to O'Rahilly, 1983.

claim: In human embryos, Ki67-positive RPE cells represented about 85-75% of the total between CS13 and CS16.
source: Owing to the difficulties in obtaining early human embryonic samples, the percentage of proliferating cells could only be estimated, showing that in the OTX2-positive domain (Figure 4, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), Ki67-positive RPE cells represented about 85–75% of the total between CS13 and CS16.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7.

claim: During human optic cup formation, the prospective RPE layer always appeared as a rather thick pseudostratified epithelium with an organization resembling that of the neural retina composed of densely packed and elongated neuroepithelial cells.
source: During this period, the prospective RPE layer always appeared as a rather thick pseudostratified epithelium with an organization resembling that of the NR composed of densely packed and elongated neuroepithelial cells (Figure 7D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: During human optic cup formation, the RPE neuroepithelium only slightly flattened (apico-basal thickness: CS13: 45 µm vs. CS16: 33.6 µm).
source: During the formation of the OC, the RPE neuroepithelium only slightly flattened (apico-basal thickness: CS13: 45 µm vs. CS16: 33.6 µm), far from reaching the cuboidal appearance seen at postnatal ages (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of sufficient time for cell proliferation, flattening is an efficient solution adopted by zebrafish RPE cells to enlarge the whole tissue to the extent needed for optic vesicle folding.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that, in the absence of sufficient time for cell proliferation, flattening is an efficient solution adopted by zebrafish RPE cells to enlarge the whole tissue to the extent needed for OV folding.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the comparative analysis across species.

claim: In vertebrates with slower development that allows for more rounds of cell division, the RPE grows in a conventional proliferation-based mode that correlates with a less evident flattening of RPE cells.
source: In other vertebrates, in which slower development allows for more rounds of cell division, the RPE grows in a conventional proliferation-based mode that correlates with a less evident flattening of RPE cells (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 7F.

claim: The cup shape of the vertebrate eye is thought to optimize vision.
source: The cup shape of the vertebrate eye is thought to optimize vision (Goldsmith, 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Goldsmith, 1990.

claim: The Tg(E1-bhlhe40:GFP) line serves as an early tissue-specific marker that precedes the appearance of previously accepted Otx or Mitf tissue specifiers.
source: Thus, the Tg(E1-bhlhe40:GFP) line serves as an early tissue-specific marker that even precedes the appearance of previously accepted Otx or Mitf tissue specifiers, as confirmed in a parallel transcriptomic analysis (Buono et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Buono et al., 2021.

claim: Bhlhe40 expression in the RPE is conserved at least in mouse and humans.
source: Bhlhe40 expression in the RPE is conserved at least in mouse and humans (Buono et al., 2021; Cohen-Tayar et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2019), suggesting a possible relevant function in this tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Buono et al., 2021, Cohen-Tayar et al., 2018, and Hu et al., 2019.

claim: CRISP/Cas9 inactivation of bhlhe40, alone or in conjunction with bhlhe41, mitfa, and mitfb, had no evident consequences on zebrafish RPE development.
source: However, its CRISP/Cas9 inactivation, alone or in conjunction with that of the related bhlhe41, mitfa, and mitfb, had no evident consequences on zebrafish RPE development, at least in our hands (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an experimental observation.

claim: Zebrafish RPE specification occurs 'en bloc' with an almost simultaneous activation of all differentiation genes.
source: However, we favour the alternative possibility that zebrafish RPE specification does not occur stepwise as in other species (Martinez-Morales et al., 2004; Fuhrmann et al., 2014) but 'en bloc' with an almost simultaneous activation of all differentiation genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a hypothesis with citations to Martinez-Morales et al., 2004 and Fuhrmann et al., 2014.

claim: By the time the optic vesicle starts to bend, the large majority of RPE cells have already left the cell cycle and have acquired a differentiated squamous morphology.
source: Indeed, we and others Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017 have shown that, by the time the OV starts to bend, the large majority of RPE cells have already left the cell cycle and have acquired a differentiated squamous morphology by undergoing a marked surface enlargement in the medio-lateral direction and a reduction of the apico-basal axis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Cechmanek and McFarlane, 2017.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis shows that during 16 to 18 hpf, RPE cells repress genes characteristic of 16 hpf optic vesicle progenitors, such as vsx1.
source: Consistently, transcriptomic analysis shows that during this same lag of time, RPE cells repress genes characteristic of 16 hpf OV progenitors, such as vsx1, and acquire the expression of RPE-specific genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion referring to transcriptomic analysis.

claim: During 16 to 18 hpf, RPE cells acquire the expression of RPE-specific genes including blocks of transcription factors and several cytoskeletal components.
source: Consistently, transcriptomic analysis shows that during this same lag of time, RPE cells repress genes characteristic of 16 hpf OV progenitors, such as vsx1, and acquire the expression of RPE-specific genes. These include blocks of transcription factors, such as known RPE specifiers (i.e. otx, mitf) and regulators of epidermal specification (i.e. tfap family members, known regulator of keratin gene expression; Leask et al., 1991) as well as several cytoskeletal components, most prominently a large number of keratins and other desmosomal components found in squamous epithelia (Buono et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Leask et al., 1991 and Buono et al., 2021.

claim: In just few hours (from 16 to 18 hpf) RPE cells acquire the molecular machinery required for their conversion from a neuroepithelial to a squamous and likely highly coupled epithelium.
source: Thus, in just few hours (from 16 to 18 hpf) RPE cells acquire the molecular machinery required for their conversion from a neuroepithelial to a squamous and likely highly coupled epithelium.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the transcriptomic and morphological data.

claim: Local interference with actomyosin or microtubule dynamics is sufficient to retain RPE cells into a cuboidal or neuroepithelial configuration, respectively, without affecting their specification.
source: Indeed, local interference with actomyosin or microtubule dynamics is sufficient to retain RPE cells into a cuboidal or neuroepithelial configuration, respectively, without affecting their specification.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing the experimental findings.

claim: Localized interference with NR bending has no effect on RPE flattening.
source: In contrast, localized interference with NR bending has no effect on RPE flattening.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion summarizing the experimental findings.

claim: The RPE acts in a 'syncytial-like' manner, as mosaic interference with microtubule polymerization seems to impact in the shape of the adjacent cells if not on the entire tissue.
source: Notably, our studies also suggest that the RPE acts in a 'syncytial-like' manner, as mosaic interference with microtubule polymerization seems to impact in the shape of the adjacent cells if not on the entire tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Mature RPE cells have been reported to be chemically coupled.
source: This is perhaps not surprising given that mature RPE cells have been reported to be chemically coupled (Pearson et al., 2004; Bao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Pearson et al., 2004 and Bao et al., 2019.

claim: The presumptive RPE of the chick and zebrafish expresses high levels of connexion proteins (i.e. Gap-43).
source: Furthermore, the presumptive RPE of the chick (unpublished observations) and zebrafish (Buono et al., 2021) expresses high levels of connexion proteins (i.e. Gap-43), which are responsible for the 'syncytial-like' behaviour observed in brain astrocytes (Buskila et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Buono et al., 2021 and Buskila et al., 2019.

claim: St18 RPE cells express many desmosomal proteins.
source: This together with the additional observation that st18 RPE cells express many desmosomal proteins (Buono et al., 2021) indicate that the tissue becomes tightly connected very soon, perhaps behaving as a community (Gurdon, 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Buono et al., 2021 and Gurdon, 1988.

claim: A flat morphology is associated with the presence of acto-myosin stress fibres that compress the nucleus.
source: In other contexts, a flat morphology is associated with the presence of acto-myosin stress fibres that compress the nucleus (Tee et al., 2011; Vishavkarma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Tee et al., 2011 and Vishavkarma et al., 2014.

claim: Myosin II is essential for the compressive role of stress fibres and its inhibition with blebbistatin causes the loss of the flat morphology.
source: Myosin II is essential for this compressive role and its inhibition with blebbistatin causes the loss of the flat morphology (Tee et al., 2011; Vishavkarma et al., 2014), as we have observed in blebbistatin- and Ableb-treated embryos.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Tee et al., 2011 and Vishavkarma et al., 2014.

claim: In Drosophila amnioserosa, actin accumulation at the apical edge seems to provide resistance to the elongation of microtubules, which thus bend, leading to a 90° rotation of all subcellular components.
source: In these cells, actin accumulation at the apical edge seems to provide resistance to the elongation of microtubules, which thus bend, leading to a 90° rotation of all subcellular components.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion referring to the Drosophila amnioserosa model.

claim: In Drosophila amnioserosa, the 90° rotation of subcellular components is accompanied by a myosin-dependent remodelling of the adherens junctions.
source: This rotation is accompanied by a myosin-dependent remodelling of the adherens junctions (Pope and Harris, 2008), a process that may also take place during RPE flattening.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Pope and Harris, 2008.

claim: Cytoskeletal dynamics occurs in a tissue autonomous manner in the RPE.
source: Although additional studies are needed to clarify the precise dynamics of the cytoskeletal reorganization underlying RPE differentiation, our study demonstrates that cytoskeletal dynamics occurs in a tissue autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Failure of RPE flattening in small regions was sufficient to decrease optic vesicle folding.
source: It was thus rather remarkable to observe that failure of RPE flattening in small regions was sufficient to decrease OV folding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation from the photoactivable blebbistatin experiments.

claim: RPE stretching represents an additional and relevant mechanical force that, together with retinal basal constriction and rim involution, contributes to zebrafish eye morphogenesis.
source: This suggests that RPE stretching represents an additional and relevant mechanical force that, together with retinal basal constriction and rim involution, contributes to zebrafish eye morphogenesis (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 8A.

claim: RPE flattening and stretching together with a substantial expression of keratins may confer a particular mechanical strength to the zebrafish RPE.
source: This flattening and stretching together with a substantial expression of keratins (Buono et al., 2021) may confer a particular mechanical strength to the zebrafish RPE, which, in turn, may constrain the NR at the same time favouring rim involution (Heermann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Buono et al., 2021 and Heermann et al., 2015.

claim: Rim involution has been reported only in teleost species where it may represent a fast mode of increasing the surface of the inner layer of the optic vesicle, thus favouring its bending.
source: So far, rim involution has been reported only in teleost species where it may represent a fast mode of increasing the surface of the inner layer of the OV, thus favouring its bending (Sidhaye and Norden, 2017; Heermann et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Sidhaye and Norden, 2017, Heermann et al., 2015, and Kwan et al., 2012.

claim: Between 16 and 27 hpf the number of cells in the outer layer of the zebrafish optic vesicle decreases from about 587 to 432, whereas that of the inner layer increases in a way that cannot be explained solely by proliferation.
source: This idea is well in agreement with previous data showing that between 16 and 27 hpf the number of cells in the outer layer of the OV decreases from about 587 to 432, whereas that of the inner layer increases in a way that cannot be explained solely by proliferation (Zheng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a citation to Zheng et al., 2000.

claim: In mammals, full commitment of the optic vesicle outer layer to an RPE identity may occur over a prolonged period of time and not 'en bloc' as in zebrafish.
source: Thus, in mammals, full commitment of the OV outer layer to an RPE identity may occur over a prolonged period of time and not 'en bloc' as in zebrafish, as suggested by comparing RNA-seq data of RPE cells from human CS13–16 embryos (Hu et al., 2019) with those from equivalent stages in zebrafish (Buono et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Hu et al., 2019 and Buono et al., 2021.

claim: Human RPE cells from CS13 to CS16 embryos are still enriched in the expression of proliferation associated genes but not of those typical of squamous epithelia as in zebrafish.
source: Human RPE cells from CS13 to CS16 embryos are still enriched in the expression of proliferation associated genes (Hu et al., 2019) but not of those typical of squamous epithelia as in zebrafish (Buono et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Hu et al., 2019 and Buono et al., 2021.

claim: A slow acquisition of RPE identity may explain why, in mice, inactivation of genes such as Otx2, Mitf, or Yap causes the RPE layer to adopt neural retina characteristics.
source: A slow acquisition of RPE identity may also explain why, in mice, inactivation of genes such as Otx2, Mitf, or Yap causes the RPE layer to adopt NR characteristic (Martinez-Morales et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2016; Nguyen and Arnheiter, 2000), whereas this feature that has never been reported after equivalent manipulations in zebrafish (Lane and Lister, 2012; Miesfeld et al., 2015), or why FGF8 can push the amniote but not the zebrafish RPE layer to acquire an NR identity (Martinez-Morales et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with multiple citations supporting the comparison.

claim: RPE cell stretching vs. cell addition are different solutions adopted by species with different rates of development to reach a common goal: an appropriate equilibrium between the surface of the RPE and that of the neural retina.
source: We thus propose that RPE cell stretching vs. cell addition are different solutions adopted by species with different rates of development to reach a common goal: an appropriate equilibrium between the surface of the RPE and that of the NR.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the comparative analysis.

claim: An equilibrium between the surface of the RPE and that of the neural retina is a prerequisite for proper optic vesicle folding.
source: Indeed, the present study together with previous observations (Carpenter et al., 2015) and in silico models (Okuda et al., 2018; Eiraku et al., 2012) support that this equilibrium is a prerequisite for proper OV folding.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion with citations to Carpenter et al., 2015, Okuda et al., 2018, and Eiraku et al., 2012.
